lead: A centrifugal pump impeller adds energy to water. The energy per unit weight added by the impeller is the Euler head. Only part of it appears as useful pressure rise across the pump. Hydraulic losses inside the impeller and casing — vane and casing friction, shock at entry and exit, and eddy formation — reduce the head per unit weight. Leakage lowers the delivered discharge; mechanical losses waste part of the shaft power. Neither lowers the head per unit weight. This chapter separates Euler head, manometric head and the main efficiencies. It gives the velocity-triangle formula for impeller work and shows why manometric head is smaller than Euler head. Only a few universities teach the full derivation.
prereq: You need: 7.2 for the impeller and casing, Unit 6 for velocity triangles and Euler's turbomachine equation, and Unit 3 for Bernoulli's equation.

blocks.text: Use subscript 1 at inlet and 2 at outlet. u is blade speed, V is absolute water velocity, V<sub>w</sub> is its whirl (tangential) component, and V<sub>f</sub> is its flow (radial) component. A pump impeller is a control volume.

blocks.where: H<sub>e</sub> is Euler head in m; u is blade speed in m/s; V<sub>w</sub> is absolute whirl velocity in m/s; g = 9.81 m/s².

blocks.text: Angular momentum gives torque T = ρQ(r<sub>2</sub>V<sub>w2</sub> − r<sub>1</sub>V<sub>w1</sub>). Power is Tω = ρQ(u<sub>2</sub>V<sub>w2</sub> − u<sub>1</sub>V<sub>w1</sub>). Divide by weight flow ρgQ: work per second per unit weight is H<sub>e</sub>. Some syllabi call this work done by the impeller.
For a normal pump, inlet whirl is small: V<sub>w1</sub> ≈ 0. Then H<sub>e</sub> = u<sub>2</sub>V<sub>w2</sub>/g. Use absolute whirl V<sub>w2</sub>, not blade speed alone.

Suction head H<sub>s</sub> is the static lift on the suction side; delivery head H<sub>d</sub> is the static lift on the delivery side. Pipe friction adds h<sub>fs</sub> and h<sub>fd</sub>. The manometric head is the useful head across the pump:
H<sub>m</sub> = H<sub>s</sub> + H<sub>d</sub> + h<sub>fs</sub> + h<sub>fd</sub> + V<sub>d</sub>²/(2g)
blocks.where: H<sub>m</sub> is manometric head in m; H<sub>s</sub> and H<sub>d</sub> are static lifts; h<sub>fs</sub> and h<sub>fd</sub> are friction heads in suction and delivery pipes; V<sub>d</sub> is delivery velocity in m/s.

blocks.text: Across flanges, H<sub>m</sub> = (p<sub>d</sub>/γ + V<sub>d</sub>²/2g + z<sub>d</sub>) − (p<sub>s</sub>/γ + V<sub>s</sub>²/2g + z<sub>s</sub>), where p is pressure, γ = ρg, z is elevation and V is velocity. Hydraulic losses inside the impeller and casing make H<sub>m</sub> less than H<sub>e</sub>, so H<sub>m</sub> < H<sub>e</sub> and η<sub>man</sub> < 1.

blocks.where: η<sub>man</sub> = H<sub>m</sub>/H<sub>e</sub> is the manometric efficiency; some syllabi call this the hydraulic efficiency of the pump, while others use hydraulic efficiency for the impeller-only ratio. Other symbols as above.

blocks.text: Mechanical efficiency η<sub>mech</sub> = power to impeller / shaft power. Volumetric efficiency η<sub>vol</sub> = Q<sub>delivered</sub>/Q<sub>impeller</sub>. Overall efficiency η<sub>o</sub> = ρgQ<sub>delivered</sub>H<sub>m</sub>/P<sub>shaft</sub> = η<sub>man</sub>η<sub>mech</sub>η<sub>vol</sub>.

figure.caption: Shaft work becomes Euler head in the impeller. Hydraulic losses reduce it to manometric head; the example gives 40.8 m and 22 m, so 18.8 m is lost.

spec.title: Energy path in a pump
spec.aria: Shaft work becomes Euler head in the impeller; hydraulic losses reduce it to manometric head, and overall efficiency compares output with input.

examples.question: A centrifugal pump runs at 1450 rpm. The impeller outlet diameter is 300 mm and the outlet vane angle is 30° measured from the tangent. The radial velocity at outlet is 3 m/s. The manometric head is 22 m. Find the Euler head and the manometric efficiency. Take the inlet whirl as zero.
steps: Convert: N = 1450 rpm, D₂ = 0.300 m, β₂ = 30°, V<sub>f2</sub> = 3 m/s, H<sub>m</sub> = 22 m.
Blade speed: u₂ = πD₂N/60 = π × 0.300 × 1450/60 = 22.78 m/s.
Outlet whirl: V<sub>w2</sub> = u₂ − V<sub>f2</sub>cotβ₂ = 22.78 − 3cot30° = 22.78 − 5.20 = 17.58 m/s.
examples.check:
import math
N = 1450
D2 = 0.300
beta2 = math.radians(30)
Vf2 = 3.0
Hm = 22.0
g = 9.81
u2 = math.pi * D2 * N / 60
Vw2 = u2 - Vf2 / math.tan(beta2)
He = u2 * Vw2 / g
eta = Hm / He
print(round(He, 1))
print(round(eta * 100, 1))

traps: Do not replace V_w2 by u2; Euler head uses absolute whirl.
Do not put H_m into the Euler head formula; H_m is useful head after losses.
Check whether β is from tangent or radial; the cot/tan term changes.
η_man = H_m/H_e is not overall efficiency; multiply by mechanical and volumetric efficiencies.
Keep the inlet whirl term when it is not zero.

quiz.a: Energy per unit weight added by the impeller; H_e = (u₂V_w2 − u₁V_w1)/g.

quiz.q: Why is H_m less than H_e?
quiz.a: H<sub>m</sub> < H<sub>e</sub> because of hydraulic losses inside the impeller and casing — vane and casing friction, shock at entry and exit, and eddy formation. Leakage lowers the useful discharge (volumetric efficiency), and mechanical losses lower the shaft power utilisation; neither reduces the head per unit weight.

quiz.q: u₂ = 20 m/s, V_w2 = 15 m/s, H_m = 24 m. Find η_man.
H_e = 35 m, H_m = 28 m, η_mech = 0.92, η_vol = 0.95. Find η_o.
Inlet whirl zero, u₂ = 18 m/s, V_w2 = 12 m/s, H_m = 15 m. Find H_e and η_man.
For fixed u₂ and V_f2, what happens to H_e if outlet vane angle from tangent decreases?
quiz.a: V_w2 = u₂ − V_f2 cotβ₂; smaller β gives larger cot, so V_w2 and H_e fall.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real impellers have slip, so V_w2 is less than the ideal triangle predicts. Industry uses slip factor and CFD to predict head. Search next: Euler head pump, slip factor, hydraulic efficiency, impeller CFD.
